sections.authorBiography: Sophocles wrote his tragedies for the festivals of Dionysus at Athens in the fifth century B.C.E. An ancient summary of Antigone says he was chosen as one of Athens' generals for the war against Samos in 440 B.C.E.; Jebb treats the tradition with care and takes it to show that Antigone was known before the summer of 441 (Jebb, 1891, Introduction, § 20). He wrote Oedipus at Colonus in his last years, about 406 B.C.E., and it was brought out after his death by his grandson and namesake (Jebb, 1885/1889, Introduction, § 18). His three Theban plays were not written in story order: Antigone came first and Oedipus at Colonus last (Jebb, 1885/1889, Introduction, § 18). This app uses Francis Storr's English verse translation (1912) as edited by Standard Ebooks; line numbers are Storr's English lines, not the Greek.
sections.historicalContext: Jebb thinks the play was probably first produced at the Great Dionysia, the spring festival of Dionysus at Athens, toward the end of March 441 B.C.E., while warning that this precise date is by no means certain (Jebb, 1891, Introduction, § 19). Greeks believed that an unburied man wandered without rest and that neglecting burial offended the gods below; George Eliot adds that these beliefs are the accidents and not the substance of the play (Eliot, 1856, para. 3). A sprinkling of dust and the proper rite were enough (lines 238–240). In Attic tragedy the chorus was a group of 12 or 15 singers and dancers (Online Etymology Dictionary, n.d.-b); here they are Theban elders summoned by Creon (lines 151–154).

publicationAndReception.publication: Antigone was the earliest of the three Theban plays, though its story comes last. This app uses Francis Storr's 1912 verse translation as edited by Standard Ebooks (Sophocles, ca. 441 B.C.E./2025).
publicationAndReception.then: Greeks kept retelling and picturing the story: Jebb describes vase-paintings connected with it, including a fragment of an Attic vase of about 400–350 B.C. (Jebb, 1891, Introduction, § 17). Hegel read the play as a collision of two powers, family and the gods below against the State (Hegel, 1838/1920, sec. "The Concrete Development of Dramatic Poetry and its Types"), and Goethe wished the brother argument (lines 849–854) could be removed (Eckermann, 1850, entry of March 28, 1827).
publicationAndReception.now: Mendelssohn wrote music for a German Antigone in 1841, and the production came to Covent Garden in London on January 2, 1845 (Jebb, 1891, Introduction, § 18). Eliot (1856) argued that both sides are right; Jebb answered that the right is wholly with Antigone (Jebb, 1891, Introduction, § 7). The debate is still the heart of teaching the play.

sections.overview: After a civil war in which Oedipus' two sons, Eteocles and Polyneices, have killed each other at the gates of Thebes, their uncle Creon, now king, forbids anyone to bury Polyneices, who attacked the city. Their sister Antigone resolves to bury him anyway and asks her sister Ismene to help.

mainThemes.note: Haemon's trees that bend in a flood (lines 667–669) state the lesson Creon learns too late.
Creon fears that if Antigone wins, “I am woman, she the man” (lines 449–450).

sections.whyItMatters: The play stages a conflict that never goes away: what we owe the law and what we owe conscience and family. Hegel, Goethe, Eliot and Jebb argued about it, and students can join that argument with the text in hand.

spoilerOverview.text: Creon condemns Antigone to be shut alive in a rock-hewn cave. Teiresias warns him; he yields too late. Antigone, Haemon and Queen Eurydice die offstage (method lines 53, 1161–1162, 1175–1179, 1235–1236, 1241 and 1246–1248 are cited by line number only). Creon admits the fault is his alone (line 1210).

segments.phase: I do: the book in one passage
segments.activity: Model a close reading of one passage using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Ismene, sister of my blood and heart, / See’st thou how Zeus would in our lives fulfil / The weird of Oedipus, a world of woes” slowly and put it in my own words: In these lines Antigone speaks at a turning point of the section, which is about two sisters, one choice. Next, craft. I notice how the lines use characterization, conflict to make the audience feel the pressure of the moment on Antigone. The strongest word is “Oedipus”: the word “Oedipus” carries the weight of the lines and points to the section's big idea. Then, effect. What do lines 1–3 reveal about two sisters, one choice? My answer: The sisters embody two answers to an unjust law: open defiance and fearful obedience. Ismene's "weak women" (line 60) states her society's view of women, which Antigone's action challenges. These lines show two sisters, one choice, and that matters for what follows in the play.

segments.activity: Whole-class discussion: why the book is still taught.
segments.script: Why does Antigone still matter? Antigone is the classic debate between conscience and the law of the state, and between private loyalty and public order. Students meet the same questions in civil disobedience, protest and the limits of authority.

segments.activity: Exit ticket on the author and context (answer given).
segments.script: Jebb dates Antigone to about 441 B.C.E. and reports that Sophocles was soon chosen as one of Athens' generals. Why might a citizen-general write a play about a ruler whose law outranks family and the gods? Answer: Accept answers such as: a citizen who served the city knew both the claims of the State and the duties owed to family and the gods, and the play tests what happens when a ruler honours only one of them.

strategies.label: Wait time
strategies.howTo: Pause at least 3 seconds after asking (5 to 10 for DOK 3 and 4 questions) before calling on anyone, and pause again after a student answers so others can add on. Call on students at random, not only volunteers.

strategies.label: Think-pair-share
strategies.howTo: One minute of silent thinking or jotting, two minutes with a partner, then pairs report. Use it for every DOK 3 and 4 question so all students rehearse an answer.

strategies.label: Follow-up probes
strategies.howTo: Answer a response with a probe instead of a verdict: ask for the line that proves it, ask "why?" or "how do you know?", or ask another student to agree, extend or challenge.

strategies.label: Student-generated questions
strategies.howTo: Students write their own questions at each level (a recall, a "why/how" and a "should/what if" question), trade them, and answer a classmate's. The teacher picks one or two for the whole class.

strategies.label: Turn and talk
strategies.howTo: A 60-second partner check for literal questions, so every student says the answer aloud before one is called on.

strategies.label: Cold call with support
strategies.howTo: Call on a student by name after the wait time; if they are stuck, offer a choice of two answers or let them "phone a friend" and come back to them.

strategies.label: Socratic circle
strategies.howTo: Inner circle discusses for 5 minutes while the outer circle tracks evidence and questions; then swap.

strategies.label: Four corners / take a stand
strategies.howTo: Students move to Agree / Somewhat agree / Somewhat disagree / Disagree and must cite a line to defend the position; anyone may move after hearing evidence.

literal.label: Literal / recall
literal.scaffold: Sentence starter: “In this scene, … because the text says …”
literal.extension: Note how this detail is set up or echoed elsewhere in Antigone.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

inferential.label: Inferential / analytical
inferential.scaffold: Sentence starter: “The text says …, which suggests … because …”
inferential.extension: Test your reading against one critical approach (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) and say what it adds.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?

evaluative.label: Evaluative / synthesis / creative
evaluative.scaffold: Sentence starter: “I (dis)agree that … because …; someone might object that …, but …”
evaluative.extension: Situate your judgment in a critical conversation about Antigone: whose reading does yours support or challenge?
followUps: What is the strongest argument against your position?
What evidence would make you change your mind?

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

questioning.alignment: Questioning design (our description; see docs/questioning-alignment.md): every lesson offers questions at three cognitive levels with DOK tags, built-in wait time, follow-up probes after each answer, think-pair-share for higher-order items and a student-generated question routine, with a level-specific focus set for each of the eleven rigor levels. It is designed to support classroom observation frameworks such as the NIET Teaching Standards Rubric (Questioning indicator); it is not NIET material and is not endorsed by NIET.

segments.activity: Students write to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Project the day's bell-ringer question (each lesson of Antigone has its own). Students write silently for 5 minutes, then pair-share for 3. Call on one volunteer and one non-volunteer, and connect their answers to divine law and human law.

segments.activity: The day's key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Introduce the day's words in the sentences where they appear in Antigone. Read each sentence aloud, ask students to guess the meaning from context, then give the gloss and the word history. Students copy one word into their journal with their own sentence.

Give the 10-minute background talk from the day's lesson: what happens in this scene, the context a reader needs, and the literary elements to watch. Pause once to ask a check-for-understanding question.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud in the day's lesson.
segments.script: Read the anchor passage aloud twice. Model the three steps out loud: what the words say, what craft choice stands out and why, and what effect it has on the reader. The day's lesson gives the passage and a full written think-aloud.

segments.activity: Guided analysis of a second quotation; expected answers given.
segments.script: Display the second passage. Students annotate it in pairs using the same three steps; circulate, then take answers to the two guided questions and confirm them against the expected answers in the day's lesson.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Students annotate the scene on their own (three marks with a margin note each) and write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph on the day's focus, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions, with facilitation notes.
segments.script: Run a 10-minute discussion from the day's anchor question and tiered questions. Start with literal checks, move to inference, and end with one evaluative question that ties the scene to divine law and human law.

segments.activity: Scene quiz in the app and an exit ticket (answer given).
segments.script: Students take the scene quiz in the app, then answer the one-sentence exit ticket with a short quotation. Collect the tickets to plan the next lesson.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Restate the day's takeaway in one sentence, ask two students to name the line that best proves it, and preview the next reading in Antigone.

What does Antigone suggest about family and the State?

objectives: Students will cite at least 2 quotations, with locations, to support each written claim about what the text says explicitly and implicitly (scored on the writing-prompt rubric).
Students will trace one theme across at least 3 sections of the play in the final paper, earning at least 70 of 100 rubric points.
Students will explain how characters, setting and point of view interact in at least 3 exit tickets, each meeting the claim-evidence-reasoning criteria.
Students will determine the in-context meaning of taught vocabulary, scoring at least 80% on the vocabulary items of the scene quizzes.
Students will write an argument with a clear claim, reasons and relevant evidence, scoring at least 80% on the unit test's short-answer scoring guides.

The words “tasted” and “blest” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The Chorus sings that when the gods shake a house, ruin passes from generation to generation, as in the house of Labdacus. Zeus' power never sleeps, and hope can deceive until the ground burns underfoot.

Haemon, lines 660–661. The evidence is “Therefore, my father, cling not to one mood, / And deem not thou art right, all others wrong” (Episode 3 (lines 589–736), Haemon). This develops divine law and human law: Haemon and his father. The words “others” and “father” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Haemon, Creon's son and Antigone's betrothed, at first speaks respectfully, then urges his father to listen: the city secretly sympathizes with Antigone, and a wise man bends. Creon refuses; the argument grows bitter and Haemon leaves. Creon spares Ismene and sentences Antigone to be shut in a rock-hewn cave with a little food.

Chorus, lines 747–748. The evidence is “Lo I myself am borne aside, / From Justice, as I view this bride” (Stasimon 3 (lines 737–752), Chorus). This develops divine law and human law: the Ode to Love. The words “myself” and “aside” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The Chorus sings of the irresistible power of Love, which overcomes gods and mortals and has set son against father.

Chorus, lines 813–818. The evidence is “Religion has her claims, ’tis true, / Let rites be paid when rites are due. / Yet is it ill to disobey / The powers who hold by might the…” (Episode 4 (lines 753–883), Chorus). This develops divine law and human law: Antigone's farewell. The words “withstood” and “authority” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Antigone is led toward her living tomb. She laments that she dies unwed and unmourned, compares herself to Niobe, and argues that a brother, once both parents are dead, can never be replaced. The Chorus both pities and blames her. Creon orders the guards to take her away.

Antigone, lines 793–796. The evidence is “Was ever fate like mine? O monstrous doom, / Within a rock-built prison sepulchred, / To fade and wither in a living tomb, / And alien…” (Episode 4 (lines 753–883), Antigone). This develops divine law and human law: Antigone's farewell. The words “sepulchred” and “monstrous” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. Antigone is led toward her living tomb. She laments that she dies unwed and unmourned, compares herself to Niobe, and argues that a brother, once both parents are dead, can never be replaced. The Chorus both pities and blames her. Creon orders the guards to take her away.

Creon, lines 993. The evidence is “Prophets are all a money-getting tribe” (Episode 5 (lines 924–1053), Creon). This develops divine law and human law: the prophet Teiresias. The words “getting” and “money” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The blind prophet Teiresias warns Creon that the birds and altars show the gods' anger: the unburied body pollutes the city. He urges Creon to yield. Creon insults him as a money-getter. Teiresias prophesies that Creon will pay with a child of his own. Shaken, Creon decides to bury Polyneices and free Antigone.

Chorus, lines 1062–1067. The evidence is “Where Ismenus rolls his waters, / Where the Dragon’s teeth were sown, / Where the Bacchanals thy daughters / Round thee roam, / There thy…” (Stasimon 5 (lines 1054–1093), Chorus). This develops divine law and human law: hymn to Dionysus. The words “daughters” and “waters” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. The Chorus calls on Dionysus, Thebes' own god, to come and heal the city.

Messenger, lines 1105–1106. The evidence is “Now all is gone and wasted, for a life / Without life’s joys I count a living death” (Exodos (lines 1094–1279), Messenger). This develops divine law and human law: the ruin of Creon's house. The words “living” and “wasted” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. A Messenger reports that Creon buried Polyneices and then went to the tomb, where Antigone and Haemon had died; Haemon had first turned on his father. Queen Eurydice hears and goes silently inside; she too dies. Creon returns, admitting the fault is his alone. The Chorus closes: wisdom is the chief part of happiness, and the proud learn it too late.

Messenger, lines 1182–1183. The evidence is “A witness that of ills whate’er befall / Mortals’ unwisdom is the worst of all” (Exodos (lines 1094–1279), Messenger). This develops divine law and human law: the ruin of Creon's house. The words “unwisdom” and “witness” carry that meaning: they are the charged choices in the line, and changing either would soften the effect. A Messenger reports that Creon buried Polyneices and then went to the tomb, where Antigone and Haemon had died; Haemon had first turned on his father. Queen Eurydice hears and goes silently inside; she too dies. Creon returns, admitting the fault is his alone. The Chorus closes: wisdom is the chief part of happiness, and the proud learn it too late.

finalPaper.title: Antigone: final paper (formal literary analysis)

prompts.text: Analyze how Sophocles develops divine law and human law across Antigone. Trace the idea through at least three moments (beginning, middle and end) and argue what the ending finally suggests.
Choose one recurring symbol, image or motif in Antigone and argue how its meaning changes over the play and why that change matters to family and the State.
Analyze a central character's choices in Antigone. Argue whether the play judges that character, and how its structure or point of view shapes your answer.
Two readers disagree about whether Antigone finally endorses or criticizes its society's view of pride and stubbornness. Weigh both readings and argue for one, answering the strongest objection.

evidence.sections: at least three sections, from the beginning, middle and end
evidence.citation: Quote the reading text exactly and cite the act, scene and line (MLA style).
evidence.outsideSources: HS Senior and above: one scholarly or historical source; College Sophomore and above: two, cited in MLA.

rubric.descriptor: A specific, arguable claim that answers the prompt and organizes the paper.
Well-chosen, accurately quoted and cited passages from across the work, meeting the evidence requirement.
Explains how language, structure and literary elements create meaning; goes beyond summary.
Logical progression, clear topic sentences and transitions; introduction and conclusion frame the argument.
Formal academic voice, present tense for literature, correct grammar and MLA format.

Thesis: Specific, arguable and precise; it organizes every section.
Clear and arguable, but broad in places.
States a topic or a summary more than an argument.
Evidence: Accurate, well-chosen quotations from across the work, all cited; meets the requirement.
Accurate and cited, but clustered in one part of the work.
Too few quotations, or some inaccurate or uncited.
Analysis: Explains how specific words, structure and devices create meaning; weighs a competing reading.
Explains the evidence, with some close reading.
Mostly summary; the link to the claim is asserted, not shown.
Organization: Each paragraph advances the argument; transitions show logic.
Order is loose; paragraphs repeat or drift.
Style and conventions: Formal, precise, present tense; MLA format; virtually error-free.
Formal with a few errors that do not obscure meaning.
Informal or error-prone in ways that distract.

finalPaper.exemplar: The sisters embody two answers to an unjust law: open defiance and fearful obedience. Ismene's "weak women" (line 60) states her society's view of women, which Antigone's action challenges. The text makes this visible when it says “If in defiance of the law we cross / A monarch’s will?—weak women, think of that, / Not framed by nature to contend with men” (Prologue (lines 1–98), Ismene). Before dawn after the war, Antigone tells her sister Ismene that King Creon has forbidden anyone to bury their brother Polyneices, who attacked Thebes; Eteocles, who defended it, will be buried with honour. Antigone will bury Polyneices and asks Ismene to help. Ismene, recalling the ruin of their family, refuses: they are women and cannot defy the State. Antigone goes alone. A full paper would carry this reading through the beginning, middle and end, and answer the strongest competing reading.
